title: Hello, Python
read:
Python is a programming language that reads almost like plain English, which is why it's a popular first language. Every Python program is just a sequence of instructions the computer runs from top to bottom.

The simplest instruction is print(), which displays text or values on the screen. Anything you want to display as text goes inside quotes — single or double, Python treats them the same.

Lines starting with # are comments. Python ignores them completely; they're notes for humans reading the code.
code:
print("Hello, world!")
print('This works too')
# This line is a comment and does nothing
codeNote:
Output:
Hello, world!
This works too

quiz.q: What does print("Hi there") display?
quiz.explain: print() shows the text inside the quotes, without the quote marks themselves.

quiz.q: What happens when Python runs a line starting with #?
options: It's ignored — comments are notes for humans
It only runs at the end of the program
quiz.explain: The # symbol marks a comment. Python skips comments entirely when running the code.

title: Variables
read:
A variable is a name that stores a value so you can use it later. You create one by writing a name, an equals sign, and a value: age = 25.

Variable names can contain letters, numbers, and underscores, but can't start with a number and can't contain spaces. Python is case-sensitive, so age and Age are different variables. The convention is snake_case: lowercase words separated by underscores, like first_name.

You can change a variable's value at any time by assigning it again — the old value is simply replaced.
code:
name = "Ada"
age = 28
print(name)
print(age)

age = 29
print(age)

quiz.q: Which of these is a valid Python variable name?
quiz.explain: Variable names can use letters, digits and underscores, but can't start with a digit, use hyphens, or contain spaces.

quiz.q: After running x = 5 then x = 10, what does print(x) show?
quiz.explain: Assigning a new value to a variable replaces the old one completely.

title: Numbers & arithmetic
read:
Python has two main number types: int (whole numbers, like 7) and float (decimals, like 7.5). You can do arithmetic directly: + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, and / for division.

Division with / always gives a float, even if the numbers divide evenly — 10 / 2 is 5.0, not 5. If you mix an int and a float in any operation, the result is a float.

You can also use += to add-and-assign in one step: a variable like score += 5 is shorthand for score = score + 5. The same works for -=, *=, and /=.
code:
price = 9
tax = 0.5
total = price + tax
print(total)

score = 10
score += 5
print(score)

quiz.q: What is the result of 10 / 2 in Python?
quiz.explain: The / operator always returns a float in Python, even when the division is exact.

quiz.q: If x = 3 and you run x += 4, what is x afterward?
quiz.explain: x += 4 means x = x + 4, so 3 + 4 gives 7.

title: Order of operations, // and %
read:
Python follows the usual math order of operations: parentheses first, then exponents (**), then multiplication/division, then addition/subtraction. Use parentheses to force a different order, just like in math class.

Two operators are specific to programming. // is floor division: it divides and rounds down to the nearest whole number, discarding any remainder — 17 // 5 is 3. % is the modulo operator: it gives you just the remainder — 17 % 5 is 2.

Together, // and % let you split a quantity into "how many whole groups" and "what's left over" — useful for things like converting seconds into minutes and seconds.
code:
total_minutes = 125
hours = total_minutes // 60
minutes_left = total_minutes % 60
print(hours, minutes_left)
query: python floor division and modulo explained

quiz.q: What does 17 // 5 evaluate to?
quiz.explain: // (floor division) divides and rounds down to the nearest whole number: 17 ÷ 5 = 3.4, floored to 3.

quiz.q: What does 17 % 5 evaluate to?
quiz.explain: % (modulo) returns the remainder after division: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2.

title: Strings: creating & combining
read:
A string is text, written inside single or double quotes: "hello" or 'hello'. Strings can be joined together with the + operator, which is called concatenation — but you can only + a string with another string, not with a number directly.

To include a number in a message, convert it with str() first, or use an f-string (covered in a later lesson). You can also repeat a string with *, like "ab" * 3, which gives "ababab".

len() tells you how many characters are in a string, including spaces and punctuation.
code:
first = "Ada"
last = "Lovelace"
full = first + " " + last
print(full)
print(len(full))

quiz.q: What does "Py" + "thon" evaluate to?
quiz.explain: The + operator joins strings end to end with nothing extra added between them.

quiz.q: What does len("hello") return?
quiz.explain: len() counts every character in the string — "hello" has 5 letters.

title: Indexing & slicing strings
read:
Each character in a string has a position, called an index, starting at 0. word[0] is the first character. Negative indexes count from the end: word[-1] is the last character.

Slicing grabs a range of characters with word[start:stop] — it includes start but stops right before stop. Leaving start empty means "from the beginning," and leaving stop empty means "to the end."

Strings are immutable, which means you can't change a character in place — word[0] = "H" is an error. Instead, you build a new string.
code:
word = "python"
print(word[0])
print(word[-1])
print(word[0:3])
print(word[3:])
query: python string indexing and slicing explained

quiz.q: For word = "python", what is word[-1]?
quiz.explain: A negative index counts backward from the end, so -1 is the last character: "n".

quiz.q: For word = "python", what does word[1:4] return?
quiz.explain: Slicing includes the start index (1) and stops before the stop index (4), giving characters at positions 1, 2, 3: "yth".

title: Useful string methods
read:
Strings come with built-in methods you call with a dot, like text.upper(). Common ones: .upper() and .lower() change case, .strip() removes leading/trailing whitespace, .replace(old, new) swaps one piece of text for another, and .split() breaks a string into a list of pieces (by spaces, by default).

.title() capitalizes the first letter of every word. None of these change the original string — strings are immutable — they all return a new string, which you usually store in a variable.
code:
msg = "  hello WORLD  "
clean = msg.strip().lower()
print(clean)
print(clean.replace("world", "python"))
print("a,b,c".split(","))

quiz.q: What does "  Hi  ".strip() return?
quiz.explain: .strip() removes whitespace from both ends of the string, leaving just "Hi".

quiz.q: What does "a-b-c".split("-") return?
quiz.explain: .split("-") breaks the string at every "-" and returns the pieces as a list.

title: f-strings
read:
An f-string lets you insert variables directly into text. Write f before the opening quote, then put any variable or expression inside curly braces: f"Hello, {name}!".

You can put more than just variable names inside the braces — any expression works, including maths and even function calls: f"Total: {price * quantity}". This is usually cleaner than joining pieces with +.

You can also control decimal places inside the braces, like f"{total:.2f}" to show exactly 2 decimal places — handy for money.
code:
name = "Grace"
score = 93.4567
print(f"{name} scored {score:.1f}%")

quiz.q: If name = "Sam", what does f"Hi {name}" produce?
quiz.explain: An f-string replaces {name} with the current value of the variable name.

quiz.q: What does f"{7/2:.2f}" produce?
quiz.explain: The :.2f inside the braces formats the number to exactly 2 decimal places: 3.50.

title: input() and type conversion
read:
input() pauses the program, waits for the user to type something, and returns it — always as a string, even if they typed a number. To use it as a number, convert it: int(text) for a whole number, float(text) for a decimal.

str() does the reverse, turning a number into text so it can be joined with other strings. bool() converts a value to True or False — most non-empty, non-zero values are True.

Trying to convert text that isn't a valid number, like int("abc"), raises a ValueError.
code:
age_text = "28"
age = int(age_text)
next_year = age + 1
print(f"Next year you'll be {next_year}")
query: python type conversion int float str

quiz.q: What type does input() always return, before any conversion?
quiz.explain: input() always returns a string, no matter what the user types — it must be converted to use as a number.

quiz.q: What does int("42") return?
quiz.explain: int() parses the text "42" and returns the whole number 42.

title: Booleans & comparisons
read:
A boolean is either True or False. You get booleans back from comparison operators: == (equal), != (not equal), < , > , <=, >=. Note that == checks equality, while a single = assigns a value — mixing them up is a very common mistake.

Comparisons work on numbers and on strings (alphabetically). You can store the result of a comparison in a variable, just like any other value.
code:
age = 20
is_adult = age >= 18
print(is_adult)
print(5 == 5)
print(5 != 5)

quiz.q: What does 7 == 7 evaluate to?
quiz.explain: == checks whether two values are equal; since 7 equals 7, the result is True.

quiz.q: What does 10 != 10 evaluate to?
quiz.explain: != means "not equal." Since 10 does equal 10, "not equal" is False.

title: Logical operators: and, or, not
read:
Logical operators combine booleans. and is True only when both sides are True. or is True when at least one side is True. not flips a boolean: not True is False.

These are often used to combine comparisons: age >= 18 and has_id checks two conditions at once. Python checks conditions left to right and can "short-circuit" — if the first part of an and is False, it won't even bother checking the second part, since the answer is already False.
code:
age = 20
has_ticket = False
can_enter = age >= 18 and has_ticket
print(can_enter)
print(age >= 18 or has_ticket)
query: python logical operators and or not

quiz.q: What does True and False evaluate to?
quiz.explain: and is only True when both sides are True; here one side is False, so the result is False.

quiz.q: What does not (5 > 2) evaluate to?
quiz.explain: 5 > 2 is True, and not flips it to False.

title: if, elif, else
read:
An if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is True. The block is marked by indentation (normally 4 spaces) — Python uses indentation instead of curly braces to show what's inside the block.

elif ("else if") lets you check another condition if the first was False, and else catches everything else. Python checks them top to bottom and runs only the first matching block.
query: python if elif else statements tutorial

quiz.q: For score = 72, which branch of the example code runs?
quiz.explain: 72 is not >= 90, so Python checks the elif: 72 >= 70 is True, so it prints B and stops.

quiz.q: What keyword catches every case not already matched by if/elif?
quiz.explain: else has no condition — it runs when none of the earlier if/elif conditions were True.

title: Nested & chained conditionals
read:
You can put an if statement inside another if statement — this is called nesting, and it lets you check a second condition only after the first one is already True. Each level of nesting needs its own indentation.

Python also lets you chain comparisons directly: 0 <= age <= 120 means the same as 0 <= age and age <= 120, just shorter. Nesting too deeply can get hard to read, so it's often worth rewriting deeply nested ifs using and instead.

quiz.q: What does 0 <= age <= 120 mean in Python?
quiz.explain: Python supports chained comparisons — this checks both age >= 0 and age <= 120 in one expression.

quiz.q: In the nested example, if has_id were False, what would print?
quiz.explain: age >= 18 is True, so Python checks the inner if; has_id is False, so it falls to the inner else: "Need ID".

title: Lists: creating & indexing
read:
A list holds multiple values in order, written with square brackets: fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]. Lists can mix types and can contain duplicates.

You access an item by its index, starting at 0, same as strings: fruits[0] is "apple". Negative indexes count from the end. Unlike strings, lists are mutable — you can change an item in place: fruits[0] = "mango" works fine.

len() tells you how many items are in a list.
code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
print(fruits[0])
print(fruits[-1])
fruits[1] = "mango"
print(fruits)
print(len(fruits))

quiz.q: For nums = [10, 20, 30], what is nums[1]?
quiz.explain: Indexing starts at 0, so index 1 is the second item: 20.

quiz.q: Can you change a list item in place, like nums[0] = 5?
options: No, lists are immutable like strings
quiz.explain: Lists are mutable, so you can reassign any item at a valid index directly.

title: List methods
read:
Lists have built-in methods that change them in place. .append(x) adds x to the end. .remove(x) deletes the first matching value. .pop() removes and returns the last item (or a specific index if you give one). .sort() sorts the list in place, and .reverse() reverses it.

Unlike string methods, most list methods modify the original list directly and return None — so don't write fruits = fruits.append(x); just call fruits.append(x) on its own line.
code:
nums = [5, 1, 4]
nums.append(2)
print(nums)
nums.sort()
print(nums)
last = nums.pop()
print(last, nums)
query: python list methods append sort pop tutorial

quiz.q: What does nums.append(9) do?
options: Returns a new list with 9 added
Adds 9 to the end of nums directly
Adds 9 to the start of nums
quiz.explain: .append() modifies the list in place by adding the item to the end; it doesn't return a new list.

quiz.q: What does nums.pop() return by default?
options: The last item, removing it from the list
quiz.explain: Without an index, .pop() removes and returns the last item in the list.

title: List slicing
read:
Just like strings, lists support slicing: my_list[start:stop] gives a new list with items from start up to (but not including) stop. my_list[:3] means "from the beginning," and my_list[-2:] means "the last two items."

Slicing a list always returns a new list and never changes the original. You can also use a step: my_list[::2] takes every second item.
code:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(nums[:3])
print(nums[-2:])
print(nums[1:-1])

quiz.q: For nums = [1,2,3,4,5], what does nums[1:4] return?
quiz.explain: Slicing includes index 1 and stops before index 4: items at positions 1, 2, 3 — [2, 3, 4].

quiz.q: For nums = [1,2,3,4,5], what does nums[-2:] return?
quiz.explain: nums[-2:] means "from the second-to-last item to the end": [4, 5].

title: Tuples
read:
A tuple is like a list but immutable — once created, you can't change, add, or remove items. It's written with parentheses: point = (3, 4). Tuples are useful for values that shouldn't change, like coordinates, or for returning multiple values from a function.

You access tuple items the same way as list items, with square-bracket indexing, and you can loop over them the same way too. Trying point[0] = 5 raises a TypeError, since tuples don't support item assignment.
code:
point = (3, 4)
print(point[0])
x, y = point
print(x, y)

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a tuple and a list?
options: Tuples are immutable; lists are mutable
quiz.explain: Tuples cannot be changed after creation, while list items can be added, removed, or reassigned.

quiz.q: What does x, y = (3, 4) do?
options: Sets x to 3 and y to 4
Sets x to 4 and y to 3
quiz.explain: This is called unpacking — Python assigns each tuple item to a matching variable in order.

title: Dictionaries: creating & accessing
read:
A dictionary stores key-value pairs: student = {"name": "Ada", "age": 28}. You look up a value by its key, not by position: student["name"] gives "Ada". Keys must be unique; adding the same key again overwrites the old value.

Looking up a missing key with square brackets, like student["email"], raises a KeyError. .get(key, default) is a safer way to look something up — it returns default (or None) instead of crashing if the key isn't there.
code:
student = {"name": "Ada", "age": 28}
print(student["name"])
student["age"] = 29
print(student)
print(student.get("email", "none"))

quiz.q: For d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}, what does d["b"] return?
quiz.explain: Dictionary lookups use the key to find its matching value — the key "b" maps to 2.

quiz.q: What happens with d["c"] if "c" isn't a key in d?
quiz.explain: Square-bracket lookup on a missing key raises a KeyError; use .get() if you want a safe default instead.

title: Dictionary methods
read:
.get(key, default) safely looks up a value. .keys() returns all the keys, .values() returns all the values, and .items() returns key-value pairs together — handy for looping over a dictionary. in checks whether a key exists: "name" in student.

Adding a new key is as simple as assigning it: student["email"] = "a@example.com" adds it if it doesn't exist yet, or updates it if it does.
code:
prices = {"tea": 2, "cake": 4}
print("tea" in prices)
print(list(prices.keys()))
prices["juice"] = 3
print(prices)
query: python dictionary methods keys values items

quiz.q: What does "cake" in prices check, if prices = {"tea": 2, "cake": 4}?
quiz.explain: in on a dictionary checks the keys by default — and "cake" is one of them, so this is True.

quiz.q: What does prices["milk"] = 3 do if "milk" isn't already a key?
options: Adds "milk" as a new key with value 3
quiz.explain: Assigning to a new key adds it to the dictionary; assigning to an existing key would update it instead.

title: Sets
read:
A set holds unique values with no particular order — written with curly braces: colors = {"red", "green", "blue"}. Adding a duplicate does nothing, since sets automatically drop repeats.

Sets are great for removing duplicates from a list: unique = set(my_list). You can check membership with in, just like lists, but it's typically faster for large collections. Sets support math-style operations too, like & for intersection and | for union.
code:
nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
unique = set(nums)
print(unique)
print(3 in unique)

quiz.q: What does set([1, 1, 2, 3, 3]) return?
quiz.explain: A set automatically removes duplicate values, keeping only the unique ones: {1, 2, 3}.

quiz.q: What's a common use for converting a list to a set?
quiz.explain: Since sets can't contain duplicates, converting a list to a set is a quick way to get only the unique values.

title: for loops
read:
A for loop repeats a block of code once for each item in a sequence: for item in my_list: runs the indented block with item set to each value in turn, in order.

You can loop over a string's characters, a list's items, a dictionary's keys, or anything else that's iterable. The loop variable name is up to you — item, fruit, i, whatever makes the code clear.
query: python for loops tutorial for beginners

quiz.q: What does for x in [10, 20, 30]: print(x) print?
quiz.explain: The loop runs once per item in the list, printing each one on its own line: 10, then 20, then 30.

quiz.q: What determines how many times a for loop over a list runs?
options: The number of items in the list
It depends on the variable name
quiz.explain: A for loop over a list runs once for every item the list contains, then stops.

title: range() and loop patterns
read:
range(n) generates numbers from 0 up to (but not including) n — useful for "do this n times": for i in range(5): runs 5 times, with i being 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. range(start, stop) and range(start, stop, step) give more control.

enumerate(my_list) gives you both the index and the value while looping, which is handy when you need to know an item's position: for i, item in enumerate(my_list).

quiz.q: How many times does for i in range(4): run?
quiz.explain: range(4) produces 0, 1, 2, 3 — four values, so the loop body runs 4 times.

quiz.q: What does enumerate() give you while looping over a list?
options: Both the index and the value
A sorted copy of the list
quiz.explain: enumerate() pairs each item with its position, so you get both the index and the value together.

title: while loops
read:
A while loop repeats as long as a condition stays True: while count < 5: keeps running its block until count is no longer less than 5. Unlike a for loop, you're responsible for making sure the condition eventually becomes False — usually by updating a variable inside the loop — or it will run forever (an "infinite loop").

Use while when you don't know in advance how many times you'll need to loop; use for when you're iterating over a known collection.
code:
count = 0
while count < 3:
    print(count)
    count += 1
print("done")

quiz.q: What's the risk if you forget to update the loop variable inside a while loop?
options: The loop runs once and stops
The loop runs forever (an infinite loop)
Python throws a syntax error immediately
quiz.explain: If the condition never becomes False, the while loop keeps running indefinitely.

quiz.q: When is a while loop usually preferred over a for loop?
options: When looping over a fixed list
When you don't know in advance how many times you'll loop
Never — for loops always work better
quiz.explain: while loops are suited to situations where the number of repetitions depends on a changing condition, not a known collection.

title: break, continue, and loop else
read:
break immediately exits the loop entirely, skipping any remaining items. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next one, without exiting the loop.

Both work in for and while loops. They're often used with an if check inside the loop, like "stop looping once we find what we're after" (break) or "skip this one item and keep going" (continue).

quiz.q: What does break do inside a loop?
options: Restarts the loop from the beginning
quiz.explain: break stops the loop entirely — no further iterations run, even if there were more items left.

quiz.q: What does continue do inside a loop?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one
quiz.explain: continue jumps straight to the next iteration, skipping any code below it for the current one.

title: Defining functions
read:
A function is a named, reusable block of code. You define one with def name(parameters):, and call it later with name(arguments). Functions let you avoid repeating the same code and give a chunk of logic a clear, descriptive name.

Use return to send a value back to wherever the function was called. A function without a return statement returns None automatically. Code after a return inside the same block never runs.
code:
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

message = greet("Ada")
print(message)

quiz.q: What keyword sends a value back from a function?
quiz.explain: return specifies the value the function hands back to whatever called it.

quiz.q: What does a function return if it has no return statement at all?
quiz.explain: A function without an explicit return automatically returns None.

title: Parameters, defaults & keyword arguments
read:
A function can take multiple parameters: def add(a, b): return a + b. You can give a parameter a default value — def greet(name, greeting="Hello"): — so callers can leave it out and get the default.

You can pass arguments by position (in order) or by keyword, naming which parameter each value belongs to: greet(name="Ada", greeting="Hi"). Keyword arguments can be given in any order, which makes calls clearer when a function takes several parameters.
code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

print(greet("Ada"))
print(greet("Grace", greeting="Hi"))
query: python function default arguments keyword arguments

quiz.q: In def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):, what happens if you call greet("Sam") without a second argument?
quiz.explain: A default value is used automatically whenever the caller doesn't supply that argument.

quiz.q: What's a benefit of calling a function with keyword arguments, like fn(x=1, y=2)?
options: The arguments can be given in any order and are clearer to read
It makes the function run faster
It prevents default values from being used
quiz.explain: Naming each argument makes the call self-explanatory and means the order you pass them in doesn't matter.

title: Scope: local vs global
read:
A variable created inside a function only exists inside that function — this is called local scope. Once the function finishes, that variable is gone, and code outside the function can't see it.

A variable created outside any function, at the top level of your script, is in the global scope and can be read from inside a function. But assigning to a variable inside a function creates a new local variable by default, rather than changing the global one, unless you explicitly declare it global.
code:
count = 10

def show():
    local_value = 5
    print(count, local_value)

show()
# local_value doesn't exist out here
query: python variable scope local global tutorial

quiz.q: Where can a variable created inside a function be used?
options: Only in functions defined after it
quiz.explain: Variables created inside a function are local — they exist only while that function is running and aren't visible outside it.

quiz.q: Can code inside a function normally read a variable defined outside, at the top level?
options: Yes — global variables can be read from inside a function
Only if the function has no parameters
quiz.explain: Functions can read global variables; it's reassigning them from inside a function that needs special handling.

title: List comprehensions
read:
A list comprehension builds a new list in one line: [expression for item in iterable]. For example, [n * 2 for n in nums] doubles every number in nums and collects the results into a new list — equivalent to a for loop that appends to an empty list, but more compact.

You can add a condition at the end to filter which items are included: [n for n in nums if n > 0] keeps only the positive numbers.
code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
doubled = [n * 2 for n in nums]
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
print(doubled)
print(evens)

quiz.q: What does [n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3]] produce?
quiz.explain: The comprehension multiplies every item in the list by 2 and collects the results: [2, 4, 6].

quiz.q: What does the if part of a list comprehension do?
options: Filters which items are included in the result
Stops the comprehension after the first match
quiz.explain: Adding if condition at the end only includes items for which the condition is True.

title: Handling errors with try/except
read:
When something goes wrong while a program runs — like dividing by zero, or converting invalid text to a number — Python raises an exception and normally stops the program. try/except lets you catch that and handle it gracefully instead of crashing.

Put the risky code inside try:, and the fallback code inside except:. You can catch a specific error type, like except ValueError:, to handle only that kind of problem and let others still show up normally.
codeNote:
Output:
That wasn't a valid number
Program keeps running
query: python try except error handling tutorial

quiz.q: What does the except block do?
options: Runs only if the try block raises a matching error
quiz.explain: The except block only runs if an error occurs inside the try block — otherwise it's skipped entirely.

quiz.q: Without a try/except, what normally happens when int("abc") is run?
options: The program crashes with a ValueError
quiz.explain: Converting invalid text with int() raises a ValueError, which stops the program unless it's caught.

title: Putting it all together
read:
You've covered variables, numbers, strings, booleans, conditionals, lists, dictionaries, sets, loops, functions, comprehensions, and error handling — the core building blocks nearly every Python program is made from.

From here, the exam will ask you to combine these: reading a short word problem, deciding which pieces to use, and writing a few lines of code that produce the correct values. There's no new syntax in the exam beyond what you've already practiced in these 30 lessons — it's about combining it confidently under a bit of time pressure.
